# The Story & the Engine
"The Story & the Engine" is the fifth episode of the fifteenth series of the British science-fiction television series Doctor Who. It was first broadcast on BBC One on 10 May 2025. The episode was written by Nigerian-British playwright Inua Ellams and directed by Makalla McPherson. It stars Ncuti Gatwa as the Fifteenth Doctor, with Varada Sethu as his companion, Belinda Chandra. Guest performers include Ariyon Bakare as a villainous figure called the Barber and Sule Rimi as the Doctor’s old friend Omo. The episode also features a cameo by Jo Martin, who briefly reprises her role as the Fugitive Doctor (a past incarnation of the Doctor). Notably, The Story & the Engine made history behind the scenes: Ellams became the first Black man to write an episode of Doctor Who, and McPherson was only the second Black woman to direct the series (after Annetta Laufer in 2022). The on-screen cast is also almost entirely Black, as aside from one minor character’s appearance, no white actors feature in the story.
In the episode, set in 2019, the Doctor brings Belinda to Lagos, Nigeria – the series’ first adventure to take place in Africa. Intending to visit Omo’s popular barbershop, the Doctor discovers it has been taken over by a mysterious new barber. This sinister Barber has trapped Omo and several customers inside the shop and forces them to tell stories while he cuts their hair. The barbershop is revealed to be more than it seems: it exists simultaneously on a normal Lagos street and in a strange realm of outer space, where it sits atop a giant spider’s web-like “engine” that feeds on the stories. The Barber’s goal is to harness the narrative energy of his captives’ life stories to power this ship and reach the center of a cosmic story Nexus for a nefarious plan. Over the course of the episode, the Doctor becomes ensnared in the Barber’s storytelling trap and must confront the engine’s demands. With help from Belinda and the Barber’s own assistant, Abena (Michelle Asante), the Doctor finds a way to overload the Story Engine and thwart the Barber’s scheme. In the end, the Barber – who is revealed to be a mortal man long ago tasked with amplifying the myths of various trickster gods – stands down from his revenge plot and releases everyone. The prisoners are freed back to Lagos, the gigantic spider-ship is destroyed, and the Barber repents after the Doctor persuades him to abandon his vengeful quest. Omo and the Doctor reconcile, and the Doctor departs with Belinda, having saved the day and given the Barber a chance at redemption.
## Production
Development and writing: The Story & the Engine was conceived as a character-driven, “high concept” episode set largely in a single location. Inua Ellams, a poet and award-winning playwright known for exploring African themes, was brought on to write the script at the suggestion of star Ncuti Gatwa. This marked Ellams’ debut in television writing. Showrunner Russell T Davies, who sought new voices for the series, asked Ellams to develop a story set in a barbershop, inspired by Ellams’s own acclaimed stage play Barber Shop Chronicles. Ellams drew on West African folklore and ideas about the power of storytelling when crafting the episode’s central premise. He has cited the West African trickster spider-god Anansi as a key inspiration – originally imagining Anansi as a “hive of all stories” that never gets credit – which evolved into the character of the Barber, a mortal man who carried the stories of the gods without recognition. The script uses the barbershop setting as a metaphorical “safe space” for storytelling and community, a concept reflecting real-world barbershop culture in Black communities. The episode’s dialogue and themes emphasize the importance of stories in shaping identity and legacy, aligning with the season’s broader motif of narratives coming to life.
Casting and characters: The principal guest role of the Barber was played by British actor Ariyon Bakare, whom the production approached directly for the part. Bakare had previously appeared in the Doctor Who franchise (as the alien Leandro in 2015) and welcomed the chance to return in a more prominent role. Sule Rimi was cast as Omo, the Doctor’s old friend who runs the Lagos barbershop, and the ensemble of trapped patrons included Stefan Adegbola (as Rashid), Jordan Adene (Tunde), and Michael Balogun (Obioma). Michelle Asante portrayed Abena (nicknamed “Abby” in the story), who is eventually revealed as the daughter of Anansi and the Barber’s accomplice. In a surprise twist, actress Jo Martin appeared in a brief cameo as the Fugitive Doctor – a past incarnation of the Doctor – during a flashback sequence that shows the Doctor’s encounters with Anansi and other mythological figures. This cameo, suggested by Davies, offers a “brief glimpse” of the Fugitive Doctor’s unseen adventures and ties into the episode’s celebration of the Doctor’s expansive history. Notably, Inua Ellams himself makes a small cameo in the Lagos marketplace scene: he appears as a street trader who attempts to sell food to Belinda as she searches for the Doctor.
Filming and design: Although set in the bustling city of Lagos, the episode was filmed in Wales, with the production team recreating a Nigerian market street and barbershop within Bad Wolf Studios (Cardiff) and on backlot sets. Director Makalla McPherson described The Story & the Engine as one of the most visually ambitious episodes of the season, due to the effort of authentically depicting Lagos’s environment on screen. The art department paid great attention to detail in constructing the set: actor Ariyon Bakare noted that the designers “recreated parts of Nigeria – the colours of the walls, the red earth, and the props – with such precision” to make the setting feel real. To achieve the episode’s blend of the ordinary and the fantastical, McPherson used extensive pre-visualization and creative camera work to keep the single-location story visually dynamic. Scenes inside the barbershop were interspersed with stylized visual effects: for example, as characters tell their stories, animated illustrations and holographic images appear on the shop’s windows to depict the narratives. The production also created a CGI model of the giant Spider creature and its cosmic web. The sequence in which the Doctor opens the shop door to find a massive spider carrying the building through space was accomplished with a mix of practical set effects (wind and rigging to simulate the vacuum of space) and computer-generated imagery. McPherson said audiences can expect the episode to be “bold, poetic, and deeply rooted in culture,” blending Lagos’s vibrant real-world atmosphere with supernatural elements of fantasy and mythology.
Related media: As a tie-in to the episode, the BBC released a short prose prequel written by Inua Ellams on the official Doctor Who website. Titled “What I Did On My Holidays by Omo Esosa,” this short story (accompanied by artwork by Bunmi Agusto) was published on 8 May 2025 and recounts how a young Omo first met the Doctor during a forest fire in Nigeria decades earlier. The prequel provides backstory for the friendship between Omo and the Doctor, which is referenced in the episode’s opening scene. A behind-the-scenes featurette for The Story & the Engine was also included in the Doctor Who: Unleashed making-of series, showcasing how the Lagos market set was constructed in Cardiff and how cultural consultants contributed to the episode’s Nigerian setting.
## Broadcast and reception
“The Story & the Engine” premiered in the UK on 10 May 2025, airing in the series’ regular Saturday evening slot on BBC One. The debut broadcast had an overnight audience of 1.59 million viewers in the UK. Official BARB 7-day figures later reported a consolidated viewership of 2.70 million (including catch-up and streaming), which placed the episode at around 35th in rank for the week’s UK TV broadcasts. These ratings reflected a slight increase from the previous week’s episode, though they remained low in comparison to historical Doctor Who figures, partly due to strong competition from ITV’s reality programming that night. Internationally, the episode was released via the Disney+ streaming platform (as part of the new co-production deal), making it available to global audiences on the same day as the UK broadcast.
Critical reception to The Story & the Engine was largely positive, with many reviewers praising its creativity, thematic depth, and representation, while some criticized its pacing and execution. Den of Geek described the episode as a “poetic, daring, and visually sumptuous” installment that succeeded in keeping Doctor Who “fresh and vital” by exploring new cultural territory. The site’s review highlighted how the Lagos setting and Ellams’s perspective brought an “invigorating” energy to the series, and it welcomed the story’s celebration of the Doctor’s identity and community in a new context. SciFi Vision similarly commended the episode’s unique concept – the idea of stories literally having power – calling it “a novel idea” and applauding how it incorporated African folklore and “universal themes of belonging and community” into the narrative. The review noted that the visuals (such as the animated storytelling windows and the regrowing hair gimmick) effectively brought the imaginative premise to life on screen. However, even favorable reviews had some reservations. Both SciFi Vision and other outlets observed that the character of Belinda, the Doctor’s companion, was underutilized in this episode – spending much of the runtime off-screen – which drew some disappointment. Despite this, Critical Popcorn named The Story & the Engine one of the standout episodes of the 2025 season, attributing its strength to “the mind of a writer with a fresh perspective” and appreciating the “exciting drama” generated by its ensemble cast and folkloric storyline.
On the other hand, a few critics delivered more mixed or negative assessments. A second-opinion review on DoctorWhoTV.co.uk argued that the episode’s execution did not match its ambition. The reviewer described The Story & the Engine as “a slow-moving parade of monologues about ‘storytelling’, while forgetting to tell a compelling story of its own,” criticizing the script for heavy exposition and a lack of suspenseful momentum. This critique found the narrative too static (owing to the single-location setting and abundance of dialogue) and felt the emotional stakes were undercut by insufficient character development – for instance, the Doctor’s deep bond with Omo is stated but not shown beyond exposition, weakening the impact of Omo’s betrayal. The same review also took issue with the story’s resolution, arguing that the villains face de facto no consequences: after terrorizing and imprisoning people and “draining their personal stories for fuel,” the Barber and Abena are swiftly forgiven and given a fresh start, which the reviewer called “bizarre” in contrast to the harsher fate of the antagonist in the previous episode. Despite these criticisms, even detractors acknowledged the episode’s imaginative ideas and thematic intentions. Fans and scholars have noted that The Story & the Engine is an unusually lore-rich chapter of the series, tying together threads of mythology and past Doctor Who “story gods” (from Anansi to the franchise’s own Land of Fiction lore) into a singular narrative. While some found this dense and confusing at times, others have praised the episode for its ambition in expanding the Doctor Who universe’s treatment of myths and storytelling tropes.
In summary, The Story & the Engine was recognized for its cultural significance and inventive storytelling. It brought the Doctor to a new setting with authenticity and heart, and marked a milestone for representation both on-screen and behind the scenes. The episode’s reception underscored the balance of risks in Doctor Who’s format – some viewers were captivated by its lyrical, metaphor-heavy approach, while others yearned for a tighter plot. Radio Times, in its season roundup, listed The Story & the Engine as a “bold experiment” for the show, noting that its legacy may lie in how it inspired more diverse storytelling in subsequent series. The episode stands as a distinctive entry in the 15th series, remembered for the way it intertwined folklore with science fiction and for the conversations it sparked about whose stories get told and who gets credit in the tales that define us.

In the new series, audiences join The Doctor (Ncuti Gatwa) and Belinda Chandra (Varada Sethu) on an epic quest to get Belinda back to Earth. But a mysterious force is stopping their return and the time-travelling TARDIS team must face great dangers, ferocious enemies and wilder terrors than ever before.

### Doctor Who Reviews: "The Story & the Engine" [![Image 1](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEg22KA2SMQCjnKzFLmj4UEu6-wFnd6hQ0u4hST4rKX_09sfcYkA8mviCa31iHRU06MPek2nFPRAPmLwHNr48b21jriYDkBtnfUgWDg6q6Th4DJeZ9uwuWTOBQsNGszN_yWP0jouI44wya2yNuiDQiNq_F-CfV-hvppuIOHFRf67_pVdCw7r3VHdb7fsoBPe/w400-h200/Screenshot%20(616).png)](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEg22KA2SMQCjnKzFLmj4UEu6-wFnd6hQ0u4hST4rKX_09sfcYkA8mviCa31iHRU06MPek2nFPRAPmLwHNr48b21jriYDkBtnfUgWDg6q6Th4DJeZ9uwuWTOBQsNGszN_yWP0jouI44wya2yNuiDQiNq_F-CfV-hvppuIOHFRf67_pVdCw7r3VHdb7fsoBPe/s1366/Screenshot%20/(616/).png) It’s always at least interesting when _Doctor Who_ goes someplace it has never been before, and Africa (certainly Nigeria) has never been touched by the TARDIS. This was the right time for it, something that the Doctor even not-so-subtly acknowledges in a pretty good beat early on in “The Story & the Engine” where he talks to Belinda about how long he’s lived and how many bodies he’s inhabited, but this being the first time he has been black (a fact contradicted later this very episode), and that he has been treated differently than he used to in parts of the world as a result. And yet in Africa, he feels at home -a sentiment that Belinda relates to with her own feelings in Britain and visiting India. A black Doctor is the best excuse to facilitate black stories within the _Doctor Who_ space -something epitomized too in this episode’s construction. It is the first story in the franchise written by a black man, Inua Ellams, and only the second directed by a black woman, Makalla McPherson (after Annetta Laufer, who directed [“Eve of the Daleks”](https://reviewsofthebosch.blogspot.com/2022/01/doctor-who-reviews-eve-of-daleks.html)). And in fact, if not for a brief cameo by Mrs. Flood and an elderly woman glimpsed in a story of Belinda’s dedication as a nurse, it would be the only _Doctor Who_ episode to feature no white people whatsoever.
None of this it seems has been emphasized much by the show in the press around this series -at least not from what I have caught. Which means it hasn’t caused a firestorm (yet) from the toxic contingents of the fan-base. But also it is perhaps indicative of how organically the show arrived at this point, which I think is the goal of the representational and diversity initiatives the worst people you know keep screeching about: to make it so that these stories feel like they belong. This episode does that fairly well, in fact it reinforces some of the core tenets of _Doctor Who_ more broadly, one reason it is perhaps the best show of the series thus far. In “The Story & the Engine”, the TARDIS sets down in Lagos, Nigeria 2019 -Lagos being a particular hub of energy for the Vindicator to recharge. While there, the Doctor sets out to visit a friend -whose connection is explained by the cold open. Omo Esosa, played by Sule Rimi (who also played Imperial turncoat Gorn in the Aldhani arc from the first season of _[Andor](https://reviewsofthebosch.blogspot.com/2023/01/somehow-andor-is-really-great.html)_ \-reuniting with Varada Sethu here) was a child when the Doctor flew into his village and doused a terrible fire from the TARDIS before planting new seeds to ensure the crop grew back. Now Omo operates a barbershop and he tells this story to three friends as it plays out in crude but nice animation on a small projection screen. He has maintained a friendship with the Doctor since then and is even now expecting him, as a green light in the shop (next to a red one) seems to indicate to Omo that he will be coming soon.
Sure enough the Doctor does arrive, but on his way his suspicions are roused by missing persons posters hung around for Omo and his friends. He then finds that the shop is under new ownership of a mysterious Barber (Ariyon Bakare) and each time he cuts someone’s hair it almost immediately grows back and thicker than before. As he does this, the patrons are expected to tell a story -we hear one of Yo-Yo Ma meeting a Shaman in Botswana that ends on a cynical statement of the industrialization of the music industry (that almost feels of a timely piece with _[Sinners](https://reviewsofthebosch.blogspot.com/2025/04/those-who-are-without-sin.html)_). But it really does not matter the subject of the story, so long as it is told -and Omo and his customers appear to be trapped there. I won’t pretend as a white guy to really know what I’m talking about here, but I am aware of a certain African and black diasporic cultural significance to barbershops as spaces of social connection and storytelling -hairdressing and hairstyling itself being connected to those same things as well. And Ellams, who is Nigerian, is very intentionally bringing that critical cultural tissue into the _Doctor Who_ universe as a root to build a story out of -a story about storytelling itself, in both mythic and modern expressions. Stories as valuable modes of communication and essential outlets of culture, and the effects -metaphorical or not- of giving up one’s stories. And that is what is happening here.
The Barber has transformed the shop into some trans-dimensional vessel that feeds on stories to keep it running -ripping them out as they are told. We see this in action when the Doctor tells a bittersweet narrative about Belinda’s life as a nurse -the stories it seems all have to come from a real place. He is drained in its aftermath. The shop itself operates very much like Howl’s Moving Castle, with the red and green lights indicating whether it is situated in space or in Lagos, and though people can enter none can leave, except for the Barber and the mysterious Abby (Michelle Asante), who is linked to his plan and who the Doctor recognizes from somewhere. Eventually it is revealed that in space the shop is above a giant robot spider weaving a web from all these stories. There is actually a moment where the Doctor disbelieves Omo and his compatriots about their inability to leave, only to open the door and find this to be the reality. And each time the shop disappears from Lagos, alarm bells ring out in the TARDIS, eventually prompting Belinda to go to the shop herself (it’s honestly not really necessary for her to have been left behind to begin with this episode).
Since the teaser at the end of [“Lucky Day”](https://reviewsofthebosch.blogspot.com/2025/05/doctor-who-reviews-lucky-day.html) revealed the spider, I had a sneaking suspicion it would be related to Anansi, the famous trickster god figure of West African folklore -and sure enough the Barber reveals himself as Anansi, as well as Dionysus, Loki, and several other similar gods in various cultural traditions. And as it looked like this was going to be another one of these gods the Doctor has had to contend with lately, it is actually a nice surprise for the Doctor to immediately discredit this -having apparently met most of these gods personally and can tell the difference. I don’t know if this was conscious subversion of the villain theme that Russell T. Davies has been building, but it was nice to have that nipped in the bud right as it was getting to feel like a crutch. Perhaps Ellams also realized the connection with the spider and Anansi would be too obvious. He does lean into it though in a different way.
The truth is that the Barber was once a human who told stories to strengthen the relationship between mortals and the gods -that he was tasked with doing this for millennia, thus considering himself the reason for their continued existence, their retained cultural power. He built the web -the “Nexus” to connect stories from all different cultures for them, and wished to receive recognition for that and the stories themselves, only for the gods to rebuke him and toss him aside. And now he wants to destroy the very thing he built for them, disconnecting the gods from the mortal stories of them -his accomplice in this, Abby, is really Abena, daughter of Anansi, who wants revenge on her father for purposely losing a bet that would have had her marry …the Doctor. And that is where the familiarity comes in -a captive of her father she had heard of the Doctor and yearned for escape with him. But the Doctor wanted to lose the bet too and couldn’t afford to take her -this we learn in a neat little pan around as the Doctor explains it was when they were a Fugitive, Jo Martin showing up for a single line as that still enigmatic incarnation. Abby though rather quickly loses her investment in the ordeal on learning that severing the gods from their stories will destroy them and make the human race much culturally poorer in the process.
Abby isn’t really done right by her ignorance here, not helped by the pace of these explanations, but Asante really gives a great performance through it. In fact the guest cast here is generally very good -Bakare is a real stand-out as well; and though Omo fades into the background the further the episode gets along, Rimi builds out a richness to his faith in the Doctor and his very particular deftness at storytelling. Something that manifests too in Asante in fairness, when she tells a story herself as she braids the Doctor’s hair -one appropriately about the braiding of hair during times of slavery to pass along maps to freedom in the hairline that slavers wouldn’t notice. This of course she does to the Doctor, freeing him and Belinda into the maze of the vessel that can take them to the engine and thus stop the Barber. When they do get there, a room full of antiquities from all over, the engine appears like a giant brain that when opened up reveals a kind of beating heart -”what else is a story?” the Doctor asks, and I really like that illustration. The Barber though arrives to stop them before they can apparently do too much damage. However in a point that is a little hastily done (it’s not entirely clear when or how the Doctor did this), but he connected himself to the engine -having an immediate effect, as he evokes Ernest Hemingway’s shortest story, though via his own less bleak version: “I am born, I die.” As is easily expected for a story about the power of one’s personal story, his history then becomes a hyper-fuel for the engine and we’re treated to that screen playing a hit list of moments from across the Doctor’s life.
What is modestly less expected though, given the track of this series I critiqued only last episode, is the Doctor extending a hand of sympathy towards his antagonist, who in a moment realizes the “never-ending story” the Doctor is providing the engine will cause it to blow up. The Doctor appeals to the Barber’s former mortality to get him to open the doors and free those captive patrons, and as the latter appears emotionally dejected, willing to go down with his ship as his long-sought plans of revenge go up in smoke, the Doctor doesn’t chastise him or belittle his point of view. He emphatically tells the Barber “I want you to live” (perhaps in echo of that iconic Ninth Doctor quote that just rang in his ears). What will his six-word story be -the Doctor declares confidently that it is not finished, urging the Barber to push through his revenge, to recognize that value in stories again. It’s actually a bit unexpectedly moving. Both leave the barbershop, just as the spider is destroyed -but the web remains stable, the gods’ link to mortals through storytelling is preserved.
There are some beats on the other side of the adventure that are really warming. The Nigerians credit Abby for keeping them alive, affirming that little redemption for her by bowing to her as living symbol of their storytelling link to the divine. And there’s a moment of pathos for the Barber, whose assertion he only wanted credit for his work reinvigorates that resonance for his character. We can all relate to that desire and the frustration at how he was treated. There is the suggestion of redemption for him as well, as Omo gives him a name, Adetokundbo -after his father, and implies the two will be in business together while a subtle look suggests even some amends with Abby -who herself balks at the idea that she, a god, received critical wisdom from Belinda (that wisdom being the pretty rote adage of “hurt people hurt people”, but it works okay and this is a show for kids after all). It again just emphasizes I think the care put into this story, and if not the characters exactly than the performances of those playing them. Spare aspects of the sentiments in “The Story & the Engine” feel cheesy, but it is a cheesy I think that belongs in _Doctor Who_. While stories about the power of stories taken to such a literal degree might have a measure of pretension, when applied so vividly in this way of cultural lifeblood, and in a visual and representational context that denotes that theme, it can’t help but feel earnest. I like that this episode is a milestone but doesn’t draw attention to itself as one. I like how it relates its subjects, even in a sometimes convoluted way, as sincere expression on tradition and connection. And I like that it vindicates the Doctor as someone who helps in the end, who can still see humanity in his foes, especially after last week (there was no appeal to Conrad’s story being greater than his actions). It’s not a masterpiece, but it is the kind of episode I expected of the Ncuti Gatwa era from the start, in terms of both its texture and designs; a direction creatively I hoped to see from this show. I’m glad it has come at last. The writer of the latest adventure discusses the importance of giving credit, the Fugitive Doctor, and the episode’s connection to Dot and Bubble…

In [_The Story & the Engine_](https://www.doctorwho.tv/stories/the-story-and-the-engine), the [Fifteenth Doctor](https://www.doctorwho.tv/characters/fifteenth-doctor) visits a barber shop in Lagos, Nigeria – a place where he has found a sense of community and belonging. This is a familiar theme for episode writer Inua Ellams, who is also known for his poetry and playwriting; including _Barber Shop Chronicles_.

We spoke to Inua about how he developed this story as both a native to Nigeria and long-time Doctor Who fan, the power of storytelling, and how _The Story & the Engine_ unexpectedly connects to some of the Doctor’s previous adventures…

_**The Story & the Engine**_ **is now streaming on BBC iPlayer in the UK and Disney+ where available.**

![Image 1: Inua Ellams on the set of 'The Story & the Engine'](https://cms.doctorwho.tv/sites/default/files/2025-05/body6-DWTV-Gallery-Module-Watermark-Template-a811382903.jpg)

Inua Ellams on the set of 'The Story & the Engine'.

**The Story & the Engine** _**explores identity, community and history all through the lens of storytelling. How did you develop the idea for this episode?**_

I had been wanting to write a Doctor Who story for some time, and Ncuti \[Gatwa\] wished for me to write one too! I had a much larger story idea, and Russell \[T Davies\]'s suggestion was, “How about something set in one location?” and so the barber shop idea came about from this. I think of story ideas as different logs in a fire, you know, just waiting – suddenly there was a spark, and it roared to flame.

This story sparked from something I read in lockdown which angered me, about uncredited artistic work. I initially thought about Anansi as a character - perhaps being the hive of all stories, but never credited for it. So that was loosely where the idea began to percolate. When I read stories of Anansi as a trickster figure, and how he sometimes treated his children, I developed the idea of a mortal being the one to lift up all the gods; and that's when I settled on [the Barber](https://www.doctorwho.tv/characters/the-barber) being the one carrying this hive of stories and never getting credited for that work.

![Image 2: The Story & the Engine](https://cms.doctorwho.tv/sites/default/files/2025-05/body3DWTV-Gallery-Module-Watermark-Template-d75cbce997.jpg)

The Doctor explores a market in Lagos in 'The Story & the Engine'.

_**The Doctor lands in Lagos in 2019. It’s rare for the series to visit the recent past, is there something about that year in particular that’s relevant to you or the story?**_

We were trying to create a story that was sort of in keeping with the world of my play, _Barber Shop Chronicles_, which was set around that time. The play is centered around different barber shops across Africa and the UK – so in my ‘Inua Ellams Cinematic Universe’, this is sort of a different story in a parallel world.

I like the idea that the Doctor’s adventure in the barber shop somehow ignites the events of the play in another world – but ultimately that’s not serious, just me playing 3D chess with myself and all my different characters!

_**Are there any influences or references to Nigerian culture or storytelling/folklore that Doctor Who fans may have missed in the episode?**_

We shot a much longer sequence near the end that we couldn’t fit in; where the Doctor and [Belinda](https://www.doctorwho.tv/characters/belinda-chandra) enter the Story Engine and find items, icons of all stories ever told, in the ship. The Story Engine operates much like the [TARDIS](https://www.doctorwho.tv/characters/the-tardis) – bigger than it seems! So there are icons for everything – we mention Hemingway, there are three of his books on the shelf. We see a plaque of a bronze from Benin City, my ancestral home in Nigeria. There are gingerbread men, references to Hansel & Gretel, _One Thousand and One Nights_ – talismans to every story ever told.

Amongst those are icons specific to West African folklore, but there’s also East African, Western, Scandinavian, Asian, Indian – everything, crammed into the Story Engine. I honestly couldn’t believe the amount of detail put into that set; it was like a candy store!

![Image 3: The Story & the Engine](https://cms.doctorwho.tv/sites/default/files/2025-05/body7DWTV-Gallery-Module-Watermark-Template-0fa8cbfe24.jpg)

The Barber (Ariyon Bakare) in his Story Engine.

**The Story & the Engine** _**also has big implications for the concept of Gods within the Whoniverse. Are there any other characters of folklore you think would make for a good Doctor Who story?**_

As Ncuti has said before, I’d really love there to be an Orisha story, where the Doctor meets the West African deities. I’d also really want him to spend some time in ancient China – they have something like two dozen thunder gods! Also the Ramayana, an epic from ancient India. My friend Vinay Patel dipped a bit into Indian history with the Partition in [_Demons of the Punjab_](https://www.doctorwho.tv/stories/demons-of-the-punjab), but I’d like the Doctor to meet some of the Hindu myths and legends, there’s so much there.

_**Jo Martin makes an exciting cameo as the**_ [_**Fugitive Doctor**_](https://www.doctorwho.tv/characters/fugitive-doctor)_**! How did this appearance come about?**_

This was Russell’s idea, and I fell deeply in love with it and wanted it to happen. We just get a brief glimpse into what the Doctor was doing while she was a fugitive, there’s still so much mystery surrounding that. And in an episode that features lots of Doctors, it’s a nice appetiser for the audience to remind them that there’s someone else here with a whole minefield of adventures and stories that we haven’t dipped into.

![Image 4: Jo Martin as the Fugitive Doctor](https://cms.doctorwho.tv/sites/default/files/2025-05/body2DWTV-Gallery-Module-Watermark-Template-2f1afae09a.jpg)

Jo Martin as the Fugitive Doctor in 'The Story & the Engine'.

_**As for the Fifteenth Doctor, this episode deals quite closely with his own sense of identity and community in Omo’s Palace. How was it to explore this side of the character?**_

I wrote this episode kind of ‘in conversation’ with Season 1’s [_Dot and Bubble_](https://www.doctorwho.tv/stories/dot-and-bubble), lots of people who have seen that episode get what it’s about. The Doctor’s anger and frustration at the end of that episode – it’s why he needs a place like the barber shop, but it is also why he feels so emotional about [Omo](https://www.doctorwho.tv/characters/omo-esosa)’s betrayal in the episode. It hits really deeply for him. I often want to suggest that people watch _Dot and Bubble_ and _The Story & the Engine_ back-to-back, to really understand what the Doctor is feeling here, his sense of need and what Lagos means to him.

The opening scene, when the Doctor walks through the market and is in utter joy – I cried when I saw the rushes, because it just clicked. It’s what I miss and love about returning to Nigeria – so understanding that need within the Doctor, and seeing it play out onscreen, was humbling.

_**As well as**_ **Barber Shop Chronicles**_**, do you have any recommended stories or media for Doctor Who fans who loved this episode?**_

I wrote a book of poems called _The Actual_, and there are a couple of poems inside that book that my episode references. They’re recommended for adults as they contain strong language, but those were spinning in my head when I was writing _The Story & the Engine_.

I mention the TARDIS in one, and reference _Back to the Future_ and the quantum realm – that one’s about the birth of hip-hop, but also its relationship with West African symbolism. If you can find those poems, you might be able to read some of the seeds of my episode.

* * *

_**The Story & the Engine**_ **is now streaming on BBC iPlayer in the UK and Disney+ where available.**

_Following the review is a detailed recap. Both contain spoilers for 2.05, “The Story & The Engine.”_

![Image 1: Doctor Who](https://scifivision.com/images/articles/2021/dw205reviewrecapiconw.jpg)The fifth episode of the season of _Doctor Who_, “The Story & The Engine,” just dropped on Disney Plus. In the episode, the Doctor (Ncuti Gatwa) visits his old friend, Omo (Sule Rimi), who runs a barbershop in Lagos, however, upon entering a place where stories hold real power, he discovers that a mysterious figure known only as the Barber (Ariyon Bakare) has taken over, and no one is able to leave.

This week’s episode of the series touched on themes of belonging and community, which is universal and relevant and I enjoyed. Overall, story-wise it was interesting, and I liked it, because was a novel idea, and the notion of stories actually having true power was a unique concept, and visually bringing them to life the way they did on the screen was smart. Adding in the regrowing hair, though a bit silly, made sense with the plot and was unexpected. The creature was also very different, and I appreciated how they incorporated both African culture as well as various gods into the story. Although I’m not quite sure we needed another storyline involving the gods, this one was done in a way we haven’t seen, and I’m really curious to see why some of the barber’s “stories” involved the Doctor and what that actually means. I also really liked how this time, by the end of the episode, the villain was able to change, as was not the case last week, so it was fun to mix it up.

That being said, I have a couple problems with the episode. The main point, which is a big one, is that once again Belinda (Varada Sethu) was sidelined. We are only getting eight episodes this season and have not had much time to get to know Belinda as a companion, and once again, she was cut out of the episode almost entirely, and it’s becoming a problem. The writers want us to connect with her and her relationship with the Doctor, and viewers need the time to do that.

The other thing that irked me a bit was the Doctor’s friendship with Omo. The scene where the Doctor realized he betrayed him was emotional and played well, but the scene at the end did not, in my opinion. While I do get that the Doctor forgives people and therefore wasn’t surprised that he did, the way the scene played out at the end of the episode didn’t work for me. I bought that he was hurt earlier in the episode, but the way he just brushed it off in the end felt disingenuous.

Other than those things I mentioned, I overall was fairly pleased with the ambitious episode; however, those things meant it was good rather than great like it could have been, and with such short seasons, we need more great.

**RECAP**

![Image 2: Doctor Who](https://scifivision.com/images/articles/2021/dw205_01.jpg)A man named Omo tells a story while he’s getting a haircut at the barbershop of when he was a boy and there was a fire destroying the forest. On the interior of the window is an animation of a village on fire that changes as he talks. He says that suddenly there was a man in a blue box who put out the fire and scattered seeds who went by the name the Doctor.

He, along with three other men in the room, stare at the red light on the wall until it goes out and the green light comes on. The one man, Tunde (Jordan Adene), questions that he is sure the Doctor will come, and Omo tells him that yes, he always comes when he is needed.

Suddenly the red light goes back on and an alarm goes off, and the room shakes. Tunde says that they need the Doctor now, because it needs feeding.

Meanwhile, Belinda tells the Doctor that he needs to get her home, and he tells her he is doing all he can. Suddenly he gets an idea and wonders why he didn’t think of it before. They can boost the Vindicator if they go to Lagos, Nigeria, because it has the largest communications technology market in Africa. Plus, it’s near Omo’s Palace, his favorite barbershop. He tells her about meeting his friend Omo during a fire. Belinda questions that the TARDIS does his hair, which it does, but says he doesn’t go there for haircuts. As they land in 2019 and he takes a reading with the Vindicator, he explains that his body changes a lot. This is the first time he has had this black body, and some parts of the world treat him differently, but in Africa, in that barbershop, he’s accepted and able to forget; they treat him like one of their own. She tells him that although he may not be human, that is the most human thing and to go ahead and visit and take as long as he needs. She stays behind in the TARDIS.

The Doctor walks through the market talking to the locals, until he gets to an empty alley where he sees a sign that says to turn back. On the walls of the buildings are missing persons posters, including one for Omo. He continues until he gets to the shop, using his sonic screwdriver to scan the door.

Meanwhile, inside, Omo’s hair has grown back, and Obioma (Michael Balogun) is telling a story while he gets his own hair cut. The Doctor enters and the door slams behind him. At the same time, the cloister bells go off and everything goes red in the TARDIS. Omo says that he told them the Doctor would come. The light changes to green. The Doctor greets Omo but then notices that Obioma and the other two men, Rashid (Stefan Adegbola) and Tunde, are from the missing posters outside.

The Doctor comments on the state of the place, saying that Omo’s standards have slipped, but he says that it’s not him; there is new management. The Barber welcomes the Doctor and says that he’s been expecting him. The Doctor asks him why the street is deserted, why Obioma isn’t leaving, and why they are on the missing posters. The Barber tells him that no one can leave. Obioma says that he is the all-knowing Doctor who is supposed to save them but doesn’t know anything. The Doctor asks what he’s supposed to save them from.

The light turns red, and the alarm goes off again. The Barber asks who is next. Obioma’s hair regrows, and Tunde says that they are running out of stories. Rashid gets in the chair and tells a story, and the light turns green. The Doctor is impressed by the images on the window and says that the drawings are a visual interpretation of the story. He starts listing aliens he has met, but Omo tells him he needs to be getting a cut for it to work; it’s all connected, the windows, chairs, and clippers. The Barber tells the Doctor that he must tell a story and feed it; it’s always hungry. The Doctor asks who is hungry, and Tunde tells him that the Barber and his assistant, Abby (Michelle Asante), control it.

Abby enters bringing food and shuts the door, and the TARDIS alarm goes off again. Belinda tries to talk to the TARDIS.

![Image 3: Doctor Who](https://scifivision.com/images/articles/2021/dw205_02.jpg)The Doctor says that he recognizes Abby, but he doesn’t know from where. She scoffs and walks off. The Doctor asks what he did, and Rashid tells him that they know who he is and calls him an intergalactic busybody Time Lord, the last of his kind. Omo admits he told them about the Doctor. How could he not? He’s the greatest story he knows. The Doctor asks why he knows Abby’s face. Tunde says that she told him that they both used to work for her father, but he was mean, so they left. Now they are keeping them there until they reach their destination.

Omo tells him that the Barber turned up one day and offered to give him a haircut in his own shop. He thought it was a nice thing, so he agreed. He brought out his own clippers, and as soon as they touched him, a sort of current ran through the whole shop, and like magic, like witchcraft. It seemed to transfer itself, its soul, to the Barber. He tried to leave but his keys didn’t work. He tried to stop his clients, but the shop demanded a select few. The ones who loved the place pushed in. He has known the men there for decades, and they are like sons to him. Each of them tell the Doctor how they came to be there and who they have waiting for them at home.

The alarm goes off again. The Barber comes out and asks who’s next. The Doctor tells them they don’t have to say anything and that he will speak. When he gets in the chair and the Barber puts the cape around him, the Doctor cannot get up and struggles. The Barber tells him to tell a story. The Doctor says he’s changed his mind. Omo tells him to tell a big story, it will be easier for him.

The Doctor tells them that they want a story about Weeping Angels and Ice Warriors, but nothing is more vivid than an ordinary life. He tells them a story about Belinda and how hard she works as a nurse. The men are surprised that his pictures on the window are alive (ie a video rather than drawings). She is ready to leave for the day when the doctor calls her in to take a woman’s vitals. She notices something the doctors didn’t and tells them how to treat her. Two weeks later when leaving work, she is greeted by Mrs. Flood (Anita Dobson) and the woman she saved, who stops to give her flowers for saving her life.

The light turns green. Abby says that the batteries are full, the fullest they’ve been since the early days. The Doctor gets up and is weak. Omo helps him, telling him that the first time is the hardest, and that from now on it will be as easy as getting a haircut. The Doctor’s hair grows back. The Barber tells Omo that he was right: the Doctor’s stories alone can super-power the engine. Omo tells the Barber he can let them all go now. Abby tells the Barber that they will get there sooner, and he can finally take the throne and rule fairly. He tells her he must recalibrate the engine and check the stasis field for structural damage because of the raw power. Abby uses a remote to seal the door and then goes in the back with the Barber.

The alarm goes off again in the TARDIS. Belinda tells the TARDIS to locate the origin, and it shows her a picture of the barbershop. She rushes out into the street and through the market.

The Doctor questions that Omo planned this, and he says that he has to get the men home. The Doctor asks him if he means because he has no home, he is more expendable. He says that their families need them, and the Doctor says that he thinks because he has none that he doesn’t matter. Omo tells him that he has stories, and that is all he was thinking of. The Doctor tells him that he loved the shop; he loved him. He thought it was a home for him and he was safe. The Doctor is upset and tells them that the Barber isn’t there now so to open the door and go. They tell him that they can’t, because there is nowhere to go; it’s different from inside. The Doctor goes to the door, and Omo tries to stop him. The Doctor gets upset and tells him not to ever talk to him again. He trusted him with both of his hearts. He uses his sonic on the door as the men freak out, worried about what will happen. He opens it, and the alarm goes off, and they all grab onto something as they are pulled towards the door, the Doctor hanging onto the door frame. Outside all around is a web in outer space. The camera pulls back to show the building is on the back of a huge spider wearing a tribal mask. The Doctor makes it back inside and slams the door. The Barber and Abby come back out.

Meanwhile, Belinda walks down the alley and sees the signs warning of danger. She sees a giggling child who waves at her. She then notices the missing posters. She continues on to the barbershop.

![Image 4: Doctor Who](https://scifivision.com/images/articles/2021/dw205_03.jpg)The Barber tells the Doctor that the shop is in outer space and in Lagos at the same time and explains that the structure he saw is the Nexus. There is a time-space compressor that goes between the two places that is built into the doorframe that only lets him and Abby out, and he controls it. The Doctor asks where they are going, but he tells him he will find out soon enough.

Belinda enters the shop, and the door shuts. The Doctor hugs her, saying that it took her long enough and that he knows the alarms must have been going off in the TARDIS.

Abby knows she is the nurse from his story and asks if she is his companion and if he left her behind and told her to wait. Belinda tells her that _she_ told the Doctor to go. She then realizes they are all missing and asks the Doctor who they are, which he says he’s still figuring out.

The Doctor insults the Barber. They are all scared of him, and he hides his identity like a coward, a troll on the web. He announces that they will leave there, because there is nothing he can do; he has no real power. The Barber questions he wants to know who he is and tells the Doctor he goes by many names. As he tells the story and cuts his own hair, the window shows images again. He says he was Anansi, the man-spider, as well as other gods that he lists. He says he has been them all, in many cultures, in many worlds, in many incarnations. He says that it doesn’t matter what he is called, it matters who he is and what he does. The Doctor questions he was all those Story Lords. Belinda is also suspicious that he was all those gods, and then they both start laughing at him. The Doctor says that he is lying. He met those he talked about, including Anansi, who purposefully lost a bet to make him marry one of his daughters. He knows the gods, and he is not them. The Doctor asks him who he really is. He says that he was the one behind them all. He was once human. Whenever they told stories, the storytelling gods would grow in power. The gods needed to strengthen their bonds with humanity. He told their myths and legends and printed them, so the gods could be worshipped. They only exist now because of him and his work. He also built the Nexus. He explains that he wanted something like the brain that could expand and make connections between ideas. He took a strand of their god’s blood and essence and built a model, a web-like structure that they expanded to what they all saw outside, cross-connecting concepts, cultures, and ideas. The Doctor asks him how he collected the stories. He continues cutting his own hair as he tells him that he started small: a pub lit by candles, a Catholic church confession box, a coal-powered theater, an electric cinema, a space opera. Among the images on the window is an image of Pilazzo (see episode 202), complete with TARDIS, and a rocket that looks similar to what Belinda was taken away on in the premiere. He continues that he had the idea to power the vehicle with the stories themselves. He worked for centuries, and all he wanted was to be recognized. They told him that he should know his place. He primed the Nexus so well, that it worked without him, so they threw him out, and all he salvaged was his Story Engine. He says that he will have vengeance.

The spider stops moving, and Abby says that the engine burned too much energy holding them together when the Doctor forced the door open. Typical Doctor, irresponsible.

Suddenly the Doctor recognizes who Abby is. She is actually named Abena, the daughter of Anansi. She tells him that he is not worthy to speak her name. She grew up trapped with her father, terrified someone would win her in a bet. She heard about him traveling through time and had faith he would help, but instead he left her and humiliated her. He tells her that he is sorry he couldn’t take her with him. He remembers himself as the Fugitive Doctor (Jo Martin) and tells her that he was a fugitive back then, that her father was wrong to offer that bet, and he was busy in a different story that might be finished one day. Belinda questions he took the bet, but he tells her that he tried to lose it.

When the Doctor asks where they are going, the Barber reveals they are traveling to the heart of the Nexus. Abby says that they are going to install the shop there and make him storyteller supreme, a trustworthy and careful god. The Doctor questions he told her that, knowing he is lying, because that would make him everything he hates and despises.

![Image 5: Doctor Who](https://scifivision.com/images/articles/2021/dw205_04.jpg)The Doctor eventually gets him to tell him his plan, and he says it’s to cut all of the gods out of memory. The Doctor says that severing the gods from the story web, cutting them from their essence, will kill them. Belinda points out it would kill Abena’s father, and the Barber tells her that that is his gift to her, because of what her father did. The Doctor says that humans are tied to the gods; destroying them would harm the very essence of humanity. He questions the others knew about the plan, but they didn’t. The Barber tells the Doctor to sit and talk as the alarm is going off again. Tunde tries to convince him to sit, because they want to get back home to their families, but the Doctor says he can’t help the Barber do it. Belinda tells Abena that hurt people hurt people. She knows her father hurt her, but the difference between good and evil is what we do with that pain.

The Doctor promises he will get them home, but Obioma and Rashid ignore him, forcing him into the chair as he struggles. Abena suddenly yells for them all to stop. She says that _she_ will tell a story. She tells the Doctor to please trust her. He sits down and she braids his hair as she tells her tale. She says that in the time of slavery and deep suffering, the slaves who escaped would go back to try to free others. Slaves were not allowed to carry paper and were always searched, but the women were clever. They could make their hair into shapes and patterns and in one style it could be braided to the scalp, curving like roads or paths, so the women would weave maps into their hair and pass it on. The slave masters never checked their hair, so they shared the routes like that and escaped to freedom. She finishes with his hair.

The Doctor uses the sonic to make the lights go out and tells Belinda to follow him. They rush out the door into the back. Abena gave him the map to their freedom. He feels the braids to know which way they need to go, and they weave their way through the hallways.

The barber, angry she did this, tells Abena he is revoking her access and uses his remote on the front door. She says he lied to her for years. He says he will handle the others and chases after them.

The Doctor and Belinda follow the map to a door. Inside is a room with a bunch of artifacts from different cultures as well as the Story Engine, which is emitting whispers and looks like a huge brain. It is covered with masks, one of which screams. The “brain” opens up like a tree. Inside is a beating electronic heart that opens at his touch.

The Barber is getting closer, and the Doctor tells Belinda to go to the control desk and start ripping out all the wires. He needs to disrupt the flow of power, so he uses his sonic on the heart.

The Barber comes in and rushes over to look at the controls and tells them that they have done nothing; they are still on track. He will cut the gods off, and they will shrivel up and die. Belinda questions he did everything to kill them, and he tells her they deserve it. She tells him that’s rubbish; it’s his ego.

![Image 6: Doctor Who](https://scifivision.com/images/articles/2021/dw205_05.jpg)The Doctor asks if he wants to hear a story. Belinda tells him not to give him any more power, but the Doctor says it’s really short. He met Hemingway and challenged him to see how good he was, telling him to write the shortest story he could, which he wrote in six words. The Doctor then tells the Barber his own short story: “I’m born. I die. I’m born.” More energy is fed i to the machine. The Barber asks him how he is giving it power when he’s not connected to him. The Doctor tells him that the engine is connected to himself, his stories, his voice. He tells him to look, and the televisions that are around start going on, each showing a clip of a different incarnation of the Doctor. He tells him that his body is like a barbershop: all of them inside, telling their stories, bickering. He will not fail them. The videos are also playing on the window in the front room. The alarm starts going off.

The Barber laughs that he told a never-ending story and gave him never-ending power. Belinda tells him that he’s taken out a third of the engine; he can’t process that power. The engine could overload and explode, and they will all be sucked into space. The Barber questions the Doctor would do that, because the stories say he protects life. The Doctor tells him that that is what he is doing. If he destroys the gods, he wrecks seven billion lives. It’s between seven billion or them. He says that he controls the engine, but the Barber controls the doors and to let them out. He was once mortal. Their lives and stories will end because of him and asks if he wants that. The Barber finally takes out the control and unlocks the front door. The Doctor tells Belinda that the shop is compressing, so the corridor is now a straight line and for her to go; he’ll be behind her.

The others go through a portal in the front door into the outside world while the Doctor stays with the Barber and asks him what his six word story, the essence of his life, would be. He wants him to live long enough to write it and not to let it be how his story ends.

Belinda eventually goes through the door, yelling for the Doctor, and he comes out with the Barber at the last moment. He uses his sonic and the spider is sucked in as the door closes. The spider explodes.

Tunde thanks the Doctor for keeping his promise, then turns to Abena and says that the Doctor rescued them, but she kept them alive. He, Rashid, and Obioma bow before her. She tells them to rise and to go to their families.

![Image 7: Doctor Who](https://scifivision.com/images/articles/2021/dw205_06.jpg)The Doctor talks to the Barber, who says that all he wanted was to be credited for his work. He spent his entire existence serving the gods and asks what he will do now. He tells him to do what he does best, keep collecting stories and start his own barbershop. Omo says that there is no need, as he is retiring. He tells the Doctor that he thought he could handle anything. The Doctor says he can, because he looks after him too. Omo says that he should have protected him and that he’s sorry. The Doctor says he’s sorry too, and they hug.

Omo offers to help the Barber up. He tells Omo he doesn’t belong there or even have a name for people to trust, and Omo tells him to use his father’s name. The Barber thanks him and says he doesn’t deserve the kindness.

Belinda asks Abena what she will do now, and she says anything she wants. Belinda says she understands if she hates the Barber, but Abena says that she won’t have that in her heart, and repeats what Belinda said before, “hurt people hurt people.” She says imagine that a mortal is teaching a god life lessons.

The Barber puts back on his jacket and the Doctor says he will be back for a haircut and for the six-word story and wishes him luck. Abena leaves, and the Barber goes back into the shop.

As they walk through the market, Belinda asks the Doctor if he saw a child and tells him about the spooky kid she saw. He tells her that he didn’t see anything, but the stories were leaking out, getting mixed up. As they enter the TARDIS, she tells him that he has to tell her about Omo.

May 08, 2025

Cast member Ariyon Bakare, director Makalla McPherson and writer Inua Ellams share their experiences of _The Story & the Engine_!

In the fifth episode of Season 2, [the Doctor](https://www.doctorwho.tv/characters/fifteenth-doctor) and [Belinda](https://www.doctorwho.tv/characters/belinda-chandra) encounter a mysterious man, known as ‘The Barber ’, in Lagos, Nigeria – and he has a story to tell. Involving a dangerous barber shop, giant spiders and “a lot of hair”, the next adventure brings the Doctor to Nigeria for the first time on screen..

We spoke to writer Inua Ellams, director Makalla McPherson and the Barber himself, Ariyon Bakare, about what to expect in [_The Story & the Engine_](https://www.doctorwho.tv/stories/the-story-and-the-engine).

![Image 1: The Story & the Engine - Gallery](https://cms.doctorwho.tv/sites/default/files/2025-05/DWTV-Gallery-StoryEngine11-fa2cd9c2af.jpg)

### Ariyon Bakare (The Barber)

_**How did you come to be cast in Doctor Who?**_

It came as a wonderful surprise as they approached me directly for the part. My agent called with the offer to return to the Whoniverse. I was worried that they had forgotten I had been part of the franchise before, but then they remembered I was in full prosthetic as Leandro in [_The Woman Who Lived_](https://www.doctorwho.tv/stories/the-woman-who-lived). After my experience playing Leandro, I was delighted to step back into that world. It was an instant yes.

_**How did you feel when you were told you got the part of the Barber?**_

Thrilled! Barber was right up my alley. I was particularly excited because Inua Ellams wrote the script. His writing has such depth and cultural richness - his storytelling is poetically sublime in a way that's uniquely his. I couldn't wait to dive into this character.

_**Was it hard to keep the secret of your casting from your friends and family?**_

Absolutely. I was bursting to tell my friends but had to keep it to myself until the official announcement. I felt like Clark Kent, having the best superpower ever and not being able to share it with the world; it was fun. I’d make a great spy!

_**Were you a fan of the show before?**_

Yeah, I was a big fan as a kid. I would collect Doctor Who cards that you’d get in cereal boxes. I loved the [Daleks](https://www.doctorwho.tv/characters/daleks), of course, but I was also a huge fan of the [Cybermen](https://www.doctorwho.tv/characters/cybermen).

_**What do you think makes Doctor Who so special?**_

Doctor Who is genius because it literally built change into its story with the whole regeneration concept. More than being quintessentially British, it always stays fresh with new faces, new companions, and new creative teams. I love how it can be whatever it wants - one week, you might get a historical episode, then suddenly it's a creepy thriller, then boom - full-on sci-fi the next. But what makes it stand out is its hopefulness about people. At its heart, the show believes we can be better and that compassion and intellect matter more than violence. It's this amazing mix of wild imagination, hope, and constant reinvention that keeps fans coming back for decades.

_**What was it like working with Ncuti Gatwa and Varada Sethu?**_

You have two incredible young actors of their generation. I can only imagine that stepping into the shoes of these iconic roles, a mainstay of British culture, is quite a daunting feat. Yet together, they manage to do it with an effortless joie de vivre, making it modern and accessible to a new generation of Whovians. I love them. Their chemistry on screen is a joy to watch. Varada's smile can melt any viewer's heart. Now, blend that with Ncuti’s wit and charm, you create instant screen magic.

![Image 2: The Story & the Engine - Gallery](https://cms.doctorwho.tv/sites/default/files/2025-05/DWTV-Gallery-StoryEngine9-b4e3d7fe49.jpg)

_**What was it like working on the Doctor Who set?**_

I love the Doctor Who set; the production design is always on point. The attention to detail is incredible. When you enter the set, your first reaction is 'woah' and 'wow.' Your second reaction is, 'Where's the TARDIS?' and 'Can I get a picture next to it, on it, and inside it?' I had just returned from Nigeria, maybe two weeks before we started shooting. The attention to detail amazed me when I stepped onto the set. They recreated parts of Nigeria; the colours of the walls, the red earth, and the props were replicated with such precision that it showed how talented the production design team are and how much effort and care is put into creating an authentic setting for us actors.

_**The TARDIS lands in Lagos, a place the show has never been before; how was this to film?**_

What I love about this episode is its cultural depth. Inua's script is steeped in Nigerian culture; it tells a story about storytelling and the origins of stories - the power they hold to heal, educate, and inspire. The Nigerian cultural element is authentic; the barbershop serves as a hub of conversation where these stories are shared. Inua brilliantly employs old Nigerian folktales, those bedtime stories we all heard as children, and creates a timeless piece that is Nigerian in essence but universal in appeal. For me, it demonstrates that all stories are significant; stories are not diminished by culture, race, or geography. Good storytelling is simply that - no one story is less relevant than another. In the end, it reminds us that whether across galaxies or cultures, our shared stories are what truly make us human.

_**What else can audiences expect to see from this episode?**_

Hair, lots of hair.

_**Where would you go if you could travel in the TARDIS to any time and place in the universe?**_

This is a particularly hard question to answer. James Baldwin once said, “Once you find yourself in another civilisation, you're forced to examine your own.” With this knowledge, I travelled through so many eras via literature, art, and films. But there are many that I would have loved to inhabit physically. I’d love to have experienced everything from Ancient Greece to the Harlem Renaissance. Finally, I’ve landed on the “Années Folles" (The Crazy Years) in 1920s Paris, the Jazz Age. The civil rights era of the 1960s sits right alongside it.

_**What would it be if you had to describe the episode in one word or phrase?**_

A time-bending Cultural Ancestral Collision.

![Image 3: The Story & the Engine - Gallery](https://cms.doctorwho.tv/sites/default/files/2025-05/DWTV-Gallery-StoryEngine12-d8731eed72.jpg)

### Makalla McPherson (Director)

_**What can audiences expect from this episode?**_

Audiences can expect something bold, poetic, and deeply rooted in culture. We take the Doctor out of his usual world and bring him to Nigeria—which immediately shifts the energy and opens up new possibilities. Inua Ellams wrote a truly unique script with a very distinct tone.

The episode is fast-paced, filled with rich cultural references, and led by a brilliant ensemble cast—including the incredible Ariyon Bakare and Sule Rimi. Tonally, it dances between emotional intimacy and uncertainty, touching on themes of friendship, identity, and community. There’s also a dark, gritty undercurrent that gives the story real weight.

It was a joy to bring to life, and I’m so grateful to the team who made it happen. There were definitely some challenges in the shoot, but everyone came together with passion and care, and I’m incredibly thankful for that.

_**Can you tell us about the process of creating this episode?**_

My starting point was always the script—understanding the story beats, the characters, the emotional spine, and asking what we could show rather than tell. Most of the episode takes place in a single location—a barber shop—with an ensemble of eight strong actors. So the challenge was: how do we keep this dynamic, fresh, and visually engaging?

We used a tool called Previs (previsualisation technology), which let me step into the set virtually using a 3D headset. That meant I could block scenes, map out camera movement, understand scale, and decide where props and action would go, all before the set was built. It gave us a clear blueprint and allowed us to be bold with how we used the space.

Working with designer Phil Sims was also key—he was instrumental in helping bring the cultural world of the episode to life, with authenticity and imagination.

![Image 4: The Story & the Engine - Gallery](https://cms.doctorwho.tv/sites/default/files/2025-05/DWTV-Gallery-StoryEngine3-47774a3c98.jpg)

_**How was it to work on Doctor Who?**_

I absolutely loved it. I had an incredible time. I’ve been a huge fan of Russell T Davies for years, so to collaborate with him was a real privilege. He was supportive and generous from the start. I remember him saying, “Every episode is like a film—make it your own. Put your stamp on it.” That freedom to be expressive while still honouring the legacy of Doctor Who was amazing.

The scale of the production is phenomenal. Walking into Bad Wolf Studios and seeing the ambition behind the sets, the craftsmanship, the sheer number of people working tirelessly behind the scenes—it was awe-inspiring. And despite its size, the show really feels like a family. Everyone is working towards the same goal: to make something extraordinary.

_**How was it working with Ncuti and Varada?**_

It was a real pleasure. Varada is such a talented actress—thoughtful, open, and really collaborative. She brought so much depth to her character. And Ncuti is just electric. He’s determined to make this Doctor his own, and he brings real care and precision to every choice.

As a director, your role is to support them—guide when needed, but mostly create a space where they can shine. They were both open to collaboration and committed to delivering something special. It was a joy to share the space with them.

_**If you could travel anywhere in time and space, where would you go?**_

I’d go back in time—to the Eighties. I was born then, but I’d love to have lived through it as an adult. I love the fashion, the vibe, the energy. There’s something nostalgic about that era that feels lost today. I like the idea of slowing life down and going back to basics.

_**If you could sum up your episode in one word or phrase, what would it be?**_

Poetic.

![Image 5: The Story & the Engine - Gallery](https://cms.doctorwho.tv/sites/default/files/2025-05/DWTV-Gallery-StoryEngine6-ac3a3b7b17.jpg)

### Inua Ellams (Writer)

_**Welcome to the Whoniverse. How did your involvement in Doctor Who come about?**_

I got really excited when it was announced Russell was returning as I’m a huge fan of his work. I dropped him a message. All I said was that I’m really excited by what you’re going to do next, I’m a huge fan of your work and I can’t wait to watch the next series. Within an hour, Russell responded saying “Inua, I’m a huge fan of your work, would you come and write for us?” I said “Absolutely!”. I went up to meet him and we chatted and set up an idea, and it began burrowing away.

_**Have you always been a fan of Doctor Who?**_

Yeah, I’ve been watching since I was ten years old in Nigeria. I’m a huge fan. There was a long hiatus when there was nothing happening. Then when the show returned, I watched most of them.

_**What is the process of writing an episode of Doctor Who? Is it different to what you’ve done before?**_

The turnover time is faster. A play takes me five or six years to write, but we had to do this in a relatively short time - in about a year. It’s also very different from writing a regular drama, when much of the information and storytelling comes out through dialogue. You have to think pictorially. It took me some time to really boil down into that. I had really great script editors, particularly David Cheung, who worked with me diligently across the script. Russell’s vast knowledge and experience and input was, without a doubt, viscerally important to writing it.

I really liked working with Russell. There was something the previous showrunner said to me, Chris Chibnall, which I think is true: “Doctor Who is a sci-fi and horror for eight years old, but also for all ages.” I kept that in mind. What would terrify an eight-year-old, but what’s also fun and exciting. How do you honour as much of what has come before, whilst creating new things for a new generation? It was great to grapple with and I had so much fun.

_**What can you tease about the episode you’ve written?**_

It’s entirely set in mostly one location. The moral of the story is to give credit where it’s due. And I took that little idea and expanded it, and really drew it out. It is a huge story, but also a very simple that sits on a lot of social history. It’s one location, a lot of fun, a lot of mythology written into it, but a new myth too.

![Image 6: The Story & the Engine - Gallery](https://cms.doctorwho.tv/sites/default/files/2025-05/DWTV-Gallery-StoryEngine4-8a98d0f918.jpg)

_**What does it mean to you to set this story in Lagos, and why did you choose the barber shop?**_

I was a kid in Lagos when I started watching Doctor Who. The show taught me to really dream beyond my present reality, to go across the universe, to leap into incredible adventures. When I became a displaced person and an immigrant, I forgot about what it felt like to be in Nigeria. Sixteen years passed before I returned to visit as an adult, and something began to nestle and settle into my body.

My body remembered a way of being, a sense of freedom. So, to take Doctor Who, this Doctor particularly, to Lagos sort of felt like stretching an olive branch out to the Inua who lived there three decades ago.

I guess what I’m trying to show is a little bit of the magic of Lagos, a little bit of the sparkles that exist when you choose to discover it. Doctor Who is full of incredible stories, and this is what happens in barber shops. Incredible stories are told. So, I was trying to unite them all.

_**What was it like writing for the Doctor and Belinda?**_

Ncuti and Varada brought so much joy and tenderness to the script I had written. Early in the drafts, I tried to make fun of the fact that he’s called the Doctor and she’s a nurse, I tried to play out a sort of buddy-cop relationship, but I quickly realized, there was much more at play, and something deeper between them.

The series starts off with Belinda determined to get home, the Doctor trying everything he can to get her home, and the frustrations all that causes. There’s a shift in this. Compared to other companions, Belinda doesn’t want to go on adventures. She loves her work, she wants to do her work, she’s thrown into this adventure. Most companions decide to go with the Doctor but Belinda doesn’t have a choice. Keeping that in focus really underpinned the decisions I made about how the characters talk to each other.

_**If you could travel in the TARDIS to any time or place in the Universe, where would you go?**_

I’ve talked about going to see the Pyramids when they’re being constructed, eyeing the blueprints so we could build them now. That’s still top of my list.

_**If you could describe your episode in one word or phrase, what would it be?**_

It’s a call to artists and creatives, to always give credit where it’s due.

* * *
